paras: The lynching of two Black men at May's Lick, Kentucky, took place in early August 1880, after the two, unnamed in every report, were accused of fatally shooting Perry Jefferson of May's Lick on August 3. According to a special telegram from Flemingsburg, the men were caught and lynched soon after the shooting. The story was known only from that one dispatch, which the Cincinnati wire said carried "no further particulars," but it was reprinted as a brief in papers from Pennsylvania to California.
The only circumstance any report gives is the Chicago Tribune's statement that Jefferson "was under the influence of liquor; hence the scrape." Jefferson's race is not stated in any of the reports.

Two men described as "negroes" shot Jefferson at May's Lick on August 3, according to the Flemingsburg special. The Tribune's version speaks of "the subsequent catching and lynching of the negroes," implying a pursuit before the killing. No report says who lynched the men, how many took part, how they were killed, or exactly when and where it happened, although the news had reached Flemingsburg by the evening of August 4.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry into the lynching was found, and the wire version that ran as late as August 18 still stated that no further particulars had been received.

The Chicago Tribune printed the special on August 5 under the heading "Kentucky Lawlessness," with a deck reading "A Kentucky Negro Murders a Man and Is Lynched," which spoke of a single man although the dispatch itself said two. In the same dispatch, the lynching shared space with a report that a band of regulators in northern Fleming County had ordered Charles Marshall, a defeated candidate for state senator, and another wealthy man to leave the county, and several papers headlined the regulators rather than the lynching.

A Cincinnati version of the special ran on August 5 and 6 in the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Unionville Silver State, which printed the victim's name as "Percy Johnson." Shorter versions then went into news-summary columns, such as the Wilmington Daily Republican's, which called the two men "the murderers," and the "Late News Items" boilerplate printed in Arkansas, Missouri and Kansas papers, which said that they "shot and fatally wounded" Jefferson. Minnesota, Wisconsin and Ohio weeklies carried the item under headings such as "Recent Tragedies" between August 12 and 14.
None of these white papers commented on the lynching itself, and every version repeated the accusation against the two men as fact. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

bases: Every report says two Black men accused of fatally shooting Perry Jefferson were caught and lynched (A1, A2, A8).

A Flemingsburg special reported that the two men were caught and lynched after the shooting of Jefferson, an extralegal killing on a crime accusation (A1, A2); no report describes who lynched them, how many took part, or where and when, and all versions trace to one secondhand report with 'No further particulars' (A2, A16).
All the reports derive from one Flemingsburg special telegram relayed through Cincinnati (A1, A2, A16); the brief versions add no independent detail (A8, A10).

accounts.gist: Two negroes fatally shot Perry Jefferson at May's Lick on August 3 and were then caught and lynched; no further particulars. The Tribune version adds that Jefferson was drunk, 'hence the scrape'.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran the special under 'Kentucky Lawlessness' with the deck 'A Kentucky Negro Murders a Man and Is Lynched', treating the shooting as murder and the lynching as its sequel.
Most papers reduced the story to a one-sentence brief in news-summary or 'Recent Tragedies' columns, without comment on the lynching.
